title: Outer Darkness and Gnashing of Teeth
hook: Is weeping and gnashing of teeth the sound of eternal torture, or of regret?
tldr: Read literally, outer darkness and a furnace of fire contradict each other. In the Hebrew Scriptures gnashing of teeth means envy, frustration and regret, an ancient FOMO. Outer darkness pictures being left outside a lit night banquet: missing honor in the Kingdom, not burning forever.
big_idea: Outer darkness means missing the banquet, not burning forever.

points.title: Fire and darkness cannot coexist
points.text: The same place is called outer darkness and a furnace of fire. Fire gives light, so read literally the images contradict each other.

points.title: Burned weeds leave nothing
points.text: Even taken literally, Matthew 13 pictures weeds burned up, which supports annihilation, not eternal torment. And that chapter says Jesus spoke only in parables.

points.title: Gnashing teeth means envy and frustration
points.text: In the Psalms and Acts, people gnash their teeth in mockery, envy, jealousy and helpless rage, never from physical pain.

points.title: The ancient FOMO
points.text: Like someone who scoffed at buying Bitcoin early, the stingy and selfish will regret the heavenly rewards and rank they could have gained.

points.title: Outside the lit banquet
points.text: Banquets were held at night and were often the only light in town. Outer darkness means being excluded from the celebration, like being kept in the dark.

points.title: Missing honor, not life
points.text: In the wedding parable, all are invited but only those in wedding clothes feast. Others still have eternal life but miss the coronation celebration.

sections.summary: Out of context these metaphors sound like Augustinian-Calvinist hellfire: subjects of the kingdom thrown outside into darkness (Matthew 8:12), into the blazing furnace (Matthew 13:42), bound hand and foot and thrown into the darkness (Matthew 22:13), with weeping and gnashing of teeth. Many picture millions weeping and gnashing forever. Literally, they would need endless hydration, steel teeth replaced monthly, and decent dentists.

sections.h: Darkness and fire: a literal contradiction
sections.summary: Matthew 22:13 calls the place outer darkness; Matthew 13:50 calls it a furnace of fire. Fire produces light. The Physics Department at the University of Illinois notes there cannot be a black flame, since black means no visible light. For a first-century Jew there could not be both fire and darkness. Literally, Matthew 13:40 even supports annihilation: weeds burned up leave nothing.

Matthew 13 itself says Jesus said nothing to the crowds without a parable (Matthew 13:34), so these should be read as metaphors. Wise people, especially rabbis, speak in metaphors; the uninformed take them literally. Jesus used parables because seeing they do not see and hearing they do not understand (Matthew 13:13). Ironically, the uninformed were the most religious people. The question is what these images meant to the original Jewish hearers.

The phrase appears in the Hebrew Scriptures without pain or abuse. David's enemies gnash their teeth in godless mockery, likely jealous of the king (Psalm 35:16). The wicked plot against the righteous and gnash their teeth from envy (Psalm 37:12). The wicked see, are vexed, gnash their teeth and waste away in helpless rage at the righteous' blessing (Psalm 112:10). Sanhedrin members, frustrated by Stephen, gnashed their teeth at him (Acts 7:54). It means envy, jealousy, regret or frustration, not physical suffering.

Gnashing of teeth is best understood as FOMO, the fear of missing out on what could make life better. Picture scoffing at an early Bitcoin offer and later realizing you missed becoming a millionaire. It is not people whipped endlessly in hellfire but regret, Christians' included, over rewards and honor they could have secured. You can spend on a luxury boat or invest spiritually: feeding the poor, building wells, supporting a struggling Bible scholar in Israel.

Store up treasures in heaven, not on earth where moths and thieves destroy (Matthew 6:19-21). Give in secret and the Father will reward you (Matthew 6:3-4). Sell your possessions, give to the poor, have treasure in heaven (Matthew 19:21). I will give to each according to what they have done (Revelation 22:12). See also Matthew 5:12, 10:42, 18:4, 20:26-28, 25:21, 25:34-40; Mark 9:41, 10:29-30; Luke 6:22-23, 12:33-34, 18:22.

The stingy, mean, uncaring and arrogant will gnash their teeth in regret; the sacrificial, kind, generous and empathetic inherit the Kingdom's blessings. The coming Kingdom will likely have roles and hierarchy; it is God's Kingdom, not a communist country. Christians can secure not escape from hellfire but elevated status through sacrifice, generosity and kindness. Those whose selfish deeds put them at the lowest rank will feel remorse searing like an unquenchable flame: the ultimate Fear of Missing Out.

In the Old Testament darkness can mean despair, ignorance or exclusion from God's protection and blessing; the Torah links it to misfortune: groping at noonday like a blind man, not prospering, plundered (Deuteronomy 28:29). In the New Testament, outer darkness means exclusion from a banquet. In a first-century town at night, a banquet hall in the square was often the only light. Outside was total darkness. Weeping and gnashing is the frustration of those left out, like being kept in the dark, not eternal fire.

These images convey the distress of being excluded from the greatest celebration, like not being invited to an important gathering you feel you deserve. In the wedding parable (Matthew 22:8-14) all are invited, but the man without wedding clothes is thrown into the darkness. In Middle Eastern tradition such imagery means honor, dignity, rank and standing. Others still have eternal life in Christ's dominion but miss the coronation feast. Blessed is the one who eats at the feast (Luke 14:15).

mythfact.myth: Gnashing of teeth describes people writhing in physical torment.
mythfact.fact: In Psalms 35, 37, 112 and Acts 7 it expresses mockery, envy, jealousy and frustration, never physical pain.

mythfact.myth: Outer darkness is a literal dark corner of hell.
mythfact.fact: It pictures being shut outside a lit night banquet: excluded from the celebration, not tortured in fire.

mythfact.myth: Those thrown into darkness lose eternal life.
mythfact.fact: Those not found worthy still have eternal life in Christ's dominion but miss the coronation festivity and its honor.

In the parable, what marks the guests found worthy to feast in the celebration.

quiz.q: In the Psalms, what does gnashing of teeth express?
quiz.why: David's enemies and the wicked gnash their teeth in mockery, envy and helpless rage, not from bodily torment.

quiz.q: Why does outer darkness picture exclusion from a banquet?
options: Banquets were at night and often the only light
quiz.why: In a first-century town at night, the banquet hall was often the only lit place; outside was total darkness.

quiz.q: What modern idea is used to explain gnashing of teeth?
options: FOMO, the fear of missing out
quiz.why: It is regret over missed rewards, like scoffing at early Bitcoin and later missing out.

reflect: What treasure are you storing up now that you would regret missing at the Kingdom's banquet?
